body:
## The room, not the booth

Tauren Wells has spent years writing songs that work on a radio clock. *Here Comes the Church*, out October 2, is the first time he has put a whole live worship record in front of people. The songs come from *Breathe On It*, but the arrangements are rebuilt for a room that answers back.

### Who is in the circle

“What a Miracle Feels Like,” with Naomi Raine, is the one that already knew how to travel. “Breathe On It” is the radio cut that still has to work when a congregation is holding the last line. Tasha Cobbs Leonard and Israel Houghton do not show up as name-drops. They change the temperature of the songs they touch. Hulvey and Abbie Gamboa pull the set toward younger ears without turning it into a feature reel.

### Play it

Listen for the space between the downbeat and the shout. A live gospel record earns its keep there. If the choir is only decoration, skip it. On this one, the choir is the argument.

body:
## After the benediction

Most worship records stop when the last chord rings. *Worship Leader’s Diary*, ANTHNY’s debut, starts on the other side of that. Thirteen tracks, written and produced by him, out September 25. The question is ordinary and hard: what does the faith sound like on Monday, with no stage and no one to lead.

### What the songs are doing

He has been in other people’s records for years, including songs for Tasha Cobbs Leonard and Kierra Sheard. “Mercy” was the solo moment people already knew. The album does not try to out-shout that. It sits in contemporary R&B pockets and lets the confession stay small. A diary is not a set list. Some of these tracks would be awkward in a sanctuary, which is the point. They are for the drive home.

### Play it

Put it on after the room has emptied. If you only know him as a name in someone else’s credits, this is the record where the name has to carry a whole hour.

seoDescription: Peg Luke and Jack Luke set the old spiritual “Lord, I Want to Be a Christian” as a slow waltz duet.
body:
## A hymn worth hearing again

Hot on the heels of the Empire re-release of [Dirt Under His Nails](https://open.spotify.com/track/0vhEfvtZwG6iAYkp3vlwXT), [Peg Luke](https://pegluke.com/) is back with something gentler. “Lord, I Want to Be a Christian” is a duet with her husband, Jack Luke. It takes an old spiritual that many people sing on autopilot and makes it worth hearing again.

{{video}}

The big decision is rhythmic. Luke lifts the hymn out of its usual four-count and sets it in three, a soft waltz sway that changes the whole temperature of the song. That lilt gives the words room to breathe. The refrain of “in my heart, in my heart” starts to feel like a prayer said under the breath, repeated until it sinks in.

The voices do quiet, steady work. Peg and Jack blend the way people do after years of singing in the same kitchen, comfortable and unshowy. When they reach “Lord, I want to be more loving,” it plays like a confession shared between two people who know each other’s flaws, which is the heart of the old spiritual anyway.

The release caps a strong stretch for [Peg Luke](https://www.instagram.com/pegcornils/). She was recently welcomed into the Recording Academy’s Class of 2026. “I am humbled and thrilled all at the same time,” she said. She also has a classical side many fans don’t know about: “I am a classical flutist as well and have played 11 sold-out concerts at Carnegie Hall in NYC.”

This is a small record in the best way. One change of meter and a second voice take a hymn people know by heart and let them feel it in their heart again.

title: Switchfoot’s Forever Now: the rock record they were dared to make

body:
## The record, not the poster

Switchfoot spent a decade wandering pop corridors and alternative side rooms. *Forever Now* walks back into the loud room on purpose. Thirteen tracks, about forty-six minutes, out June 26, 2026 on By Design / BMG. This is a **music story** — a band that still believes a guitar can carry a confession.

### What the cut does

The first two singles — “Wake Up, Mr. Crow” and “Absolution” — do not ease you in. Nearly a minute of instruments before a lyric. Mike Elizondo is back in the chair, the same producer who helped shape *Hello Hurricane*, and you can hear the kinship: punch, space, a vocal that still wants to preach without a pulpit.

“Shake the Dust” is the hard one. Tim Foreman’s bass is the argument. Chad Butler’s fill before the last chorus is the period. If you quit Switchfoot after *Vice Verses* because the grit went missing, this is the track that answers you.

### Mixed genre, same confession

“Beautiful Life” is the letter in the middle of the noise — remember the light, remember you are not alone. “YFWYA” (You Forgot Who You Are) is surf-rock as identity theology: image-bearers who misplace their names. “Two Twins” is the thought experiment, two unborn voices guessing at the world. “Breaking Up Again” is a ninety-second Jon Foreman side-quest: acoustic, odd, filing for divorce from the self. Then “The Butterfly Effect” stitches the opener’s riff into the last page, the way *Hello Hurricane* used to close a circle.

### Play it

Put it on loud. Do not skip the middle. The record has no obvious dead track, which is rare this late in a catalogue. *Forever Now* is not a costume of 2005. It is a 2026 rock album that still wants the gospel in the pocket, not as a sticker on the shrink-wrap.

body:
## The record, not the poster

Reunion nights are a high wire. The room remembers a younger band. Voices drop. Chemistry is not the van-years version. Poor Old Lu still walked into Seattle’s Showbox in fall 2025 and made a live document worth keeping. *At The Showbox* is fifteen tracks, nearly fifty-nine minutes, out September 1, 2026. Self-released. No costume. A hometown room that has held Armstrong, Sinatra, and the grunge years — the right box for this psychedelic, soulful alternative faith-rock.

### What the cut does

They open in the catalogue’s strongest pocket. “Rail,” from *A Picture Of The Eighth Wonder*, still builds that long, trippy guitar weather before the lyric names Judas and the cold hands. “For The Love Of My Country” and “All Pretty For The TV” still write social critique that Christian radio mostly will not touch — wealth, performance, the dirty word of saying a thing is meaningless. The observations have not expired. They would fit a feed in 2026 as easily as a club in the nineties.

### Mixed genre, same confession

This set is a map, not a museum: “Where Were All Of You,” “The Weeds That Grow Around My Feet,” “Bliss Is,” “Revolve,” “Receive.” The closer stretch — the rainy-city irony of “Hello Sunny Weather” into the slightly goofy “Cannon-Fire Orange” — is the right kind of uncool. Poor Old Lu wrote pointed songs from a faith floor. New bands in this lane should still steal the homework.

### Play it

If you never had the records, start here. If you did, this is the lived-in version: rust allowed, keys maybe dropped, conviction not dropped. The performance will make old listeners ask for a new studio album. That ask is the point of a reunion that works.

title: John Van Deusen’s Joyful Noise Pt. 2: worship without the poster
excerpt: Twenty tracks of praise that still sound like a band, with a guest list that actually sings — Citizens, Sandra McCracken, Jon Guerra, and a choir that stops the room.
coverConcept: Official Joyful Noise Pt. 2 artwork — square album cover
seoTitle: John Van Deusen Joyful Noise Pt. 2 review | Purposetone
seoDescription: A Purposetone listen to John Van Deusen’s As Long As I Am In The Tent of This Body I Will Make A Joyful Noise Pt. 2.
body:
## The record, not the poster

John Van Deusen does not wait for a five-year cycle. After the rock record *Anthem Sprinter* (2024) he turned into a worship writer — not a costume change so much as a second language. Last year’s *Pt. 1* was eighteen songs. *As Long As I Am In The Tent of This Body I Will Make A Joyful Noise Pt. 2* is twenty, out August 28, 2026 on Anotherland. He is writing praise for Jesus first and not negotiating the rest.

### What the cut does

The songs sit closer to the congregation than his older catalogues. “Joyful Noise” (with Citizens) bounces like it could survive a radio clock. “Mountain Mover” is the quiet one that still belongs on a Sunday. “A Call To Worship” invites you in — come let Him hold you — then throws a noise-rock ending that some will skip. The invitation is the point; the scrape at the end is a taste, not a thesis.

“The Lord Our God, The Lord Is One” is scripture in the room, built for people to sing together. Ten of the twenty tracks bring guests, and they are not cameos for the press sheet: Tenielle Neda on “With Everything We Praise The Lord,” Jon Guerra, Tyson Motsenbocker, Andy Squyres, Sandra McCracken on the long “This Is Love,” Taylor Armstrong, Chris Renzema. “Jesus Abide In Me,” sung by Blake Clawson’s choir, is the outlier that still earns its four minutes.

### Mixed genre, same confession

This is folk-rock worship with indie nerves. It is more straight-ahead than Van Deusen’s earlier work, which is a choice, not a dilution. *Pt. 1* still sits a half-step above for some ears. *Pt. 2* is the longer sit — almost too long in one pass — and the spoken closer with his son is a family document more than a replay track. If you wanted honest worship that still sounds like songs, this is the stack.

### Play it

Do not treat it as background CCM. Finish a handful. Then another handful. The record rewards return listens more than a single heroic stream.

*Christian music journalism. Mixed genres. Gospel in every story.*

## The comfortable lie
